items.title: chloro
items.text:
rustfmt's output in a fraction of the time.

chloro formats Rust several times faster than rustfmt, in a fraction of the memory, and writes the same bytes as rustfmt --edition 2024. It is a module-by-module port of rustfmt 1.9.0's formatting code onto the syntax trees of rust-analyzer's parser, so it does not need the Rust compiler. It comes as a 2 MB command-line tool and as a library.

1220/1220 rust-analyzer files identical to rustfmt 1.9.0 and to rustfmt 1.8.0; default options, 0 non-idempotent 21–35% of rustfmt's wall time, one core nine crates of 215 KB–2.9 MB, --check on formatted input 8–17% of rustfmt's wall time, four cores chloro with one thread per core; rustfmt runs on one thread 4–23 MiB peak memory on the same crates 4–10 MiB on one core, 5–23 MiB on four; rustfmt 43–86 MiB

Measured on an idle four-core x86-64 Linux VM against rustfmt 1.9.0-stable, 30 timed runs per cell. The method, every workload and the limits of these numbers are on the Performance page; the conformance matrix is on rustfmt compatibility.

items.title: Getting started
Compatibility with rustfmt
items.text:
chloro's formatting modules follow rustfmt's source files (items, expr, chains, lists, comment and so on), so each formatting decision can be checked against the rustfmt code it comes from. Any output that differs from rustfmt's is a bug; the known differences are listed.

It takes rustfmt's stable options under their rustfmt names (max_width, tab_spaces, use_small_heuristics, edition, style_edition and the rest), either as --config key=value on the command line or on a Config in the library. Unstable options keep their default values. By default it reproduces rustfmt 1.9.0; with rustfmt_version = "1.8.0" it reproduces rustfmt 1.8.0, the release shipped with Rust 1.88.

The command line is not a replacement for the rustfmt binary: chloro does not read rustfmt.toml, has no --emit modes, and does not format standard input. rustfmt compatibility lists the other differences.

items.title: Changelog
items.text:
All notable changes to chloro, for people who use it. The format follows Keep a Changelog, and versions follow Semantic Versioning. chloro and chloro-core are released together at the same version.

This file is written by hand. Each crate also has a commit-level changelog generated at release time by release-plz: chloro/CHANGELOG.md and chloro-core/CHANGELOG.md.

items.title: Unreleased
items.text: The performance and conformance work of #88. Every output is identical to 0.8.0's except for the conformance fixes listed under Fixed. The measurements behind the figures below are described on the Performance page.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• The command line formats files on every core, one worker per core, taking the largest files first; --threads N sets the number of workers.
  • Files of 128 KiB or more also have their top-level items formatted on several threads, with identical output.
  • A cache of file contents known to be formatted: a later --check or --write skips them without parsing. It is keyed by the chloro binary and the configuration, lives in the user cache directory, and does not change any output or exit status. --no-cache turns it off; --cache-dir and CHLORO_CACHE_DIR move it.
  • --unit-cache, an opt-in cache of formatted top-level items, so that a changed file formats only the items not seen before.
  • The rustfmt_version option reproduces rustfmt 1.8.0 (as shipped with Rust 1.88) as well as 1.9.0, the default: --config rustfmt_version=1.8.0.
  • #[rustfmt::skip::macros(..)] and #[rustfmt::skip::attributes(..)] are honoured.
  • CHLORO_TRACE=FILE writes a per-worker timeline of a command-line run.
  • -V/--version prints the version. A build from anything but the release's tagged commit is marked as a development build, with its commit and whether it had uncommitted changes: chloro 0.8.0-dev (2f9b060, dirty).
  • chloro-core library functions: format_source_with_config_parallel (one file's items on several threads), format_source_with_unit_cache with the UnitCache trait, UnitKey and CachedUnit (reuse formatted items across calls), and parse_only. The existing functions are unchanged.
  • Release binaries for the targets GitHub's runners build natively are built with profile-guided optimisation.
  • A documentation website at https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/, and this changelog.

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• Formatting is faster. Against rustfmt 1.9.0 on nine crates, chloro takes 0.21–0.35 of rustfmt's wall time on one core and 0.08–0.17 on four. Against 0.8.0, the formatter executes 66% fewer instructions on the same files and formats 2.7 times as many bytes per second on one core.
  • Peak memory on the same crates is 4–10 MiB on one core, against 6–29 MiB for 0.8.0 (rustfmt: 43–86 MiB).
  • Nested closures no longer slow formatting down superlinearly: a 2 KB file of closures nested 16 deep takes 5.5 million instructions, against 242.5 million in 0.8.0.
  • chloro-core's runtime dependency tree is 18 crates, from 37. rust-analyzer's syntax tree crates (ra_ap_syntax, rowan) are no longer runtime dependencies; the formatter reads its own flat syntax tree. bumpalo is added; ra-ap-rustc_lexer and rustc-literal-escaper, already in the tree through ra_ap_parser, are now named directly.
  • The release profile uses fat link-time optimisation and one codegen unit.
  • A file reachable twice on the command line (named twice, or through a symlink) is formatted once.

items.title: Fixed
items.text:
Output now matches rustfmt 1.9.0 on all 1220 rust-analyzer conformance files (1219 in 0.8.0) and on all 20,540 files of a 577-crate registry corpus that rustfmt formats (20,526 of 20,536 before):

  • Nested blocks in a macro definition get rustfmt's trailing semicolons.
  • A repeat array, [x; n], is not laid out as a block.
  • Doc comments inside macro arguments are formatted as rustfmt formats them.
  • Files containing syntax rustc's parser rejects are left unchanged, as rustfmt leaves them: <-, ..a = b, a..= without an end, an ambiguous + in a type, an unbraced const parameter default, builtin # syntax, pattern parameters in an edition-2015 trait method, a misplaced doc comment, and a C string literal before edition 2021.
  • Files with syntax rustc accepts but rust-analyzer's parser rejects are now formatted: a parenthesised first bound of a bare trait object (Box<(Copy) + Send>), a float literal as a field name, a const block item, impl impl Trait {}, and an unknown literal prefix before edition 2021.
  • A panic while formatting on a worker thread is reported with its own message.

A rewrite of the formatter: a module-for-module port of rustfmt 1.9.0 onto rust-analyzer's syntax trees (#85). Output matches rustfmt on 1219 of the 1220 rust-analyzer conformance files, against 233 before.

items.title: Added
items.text:
• Config, with a public field for every stable rustfmt option and Config::set taking rustfmt's option names and values; format_source_with_config and Config are re-exported from chloro.
  • --config key=value,... on the command line, validated before any file is read.
  • #[rustfmt::skip] on files and nodes.
  • extern crate items (#80) and if let chains (#82).

items.title: Changed
items.text:
• The formatting rules are rustfmt's: files rustfmt rejects are returned unchanged, unstable rustfmt options keep their defaults, and style_edition follows edition unless set.
  • Method chains are no longer "snuggled" (#83).

items.title: Fixed
items.text: • Comments on use items are kept (#81).

items.title: Fixed

(The release-plz changelogs of both crates list this change under 0.8.0.)

items.title: rustfmt compatibility
items.text:
chloro aims to produce exactly the bytes rustfmt produces. This page lists what its output has been compared against, how the comparisons were made, and what they do not cover.

Each result below compares chloro's output with the output of a named rustfmt binary on the same source with the same options. The comparisons cover the corpora and options listed here; they do not show that chloro and rustfmt agree on every possible input.

items.title: rustfmt releases
items.text:
rustfmt 1.8.0 and 1.9.0 differ in two ways, and rustfmt_version reproduces both:

  • Formatting. A handful of constructs come out differently, for example raw labels in break 'r#a (1.8.0 drops the r#), a labelled block as a closure body, use self::self;, super let, the import order of _-prefixed names at editions before 2024, and a macro_rules! body that is a single const { .. } block.
  • Acceptance. Each release's rustfmt formats only what its own toolchain's parser accepts. For example, rustfmt 1.8.0 formats if a && let … at edition 2021 and impl !Trait {}, which 1.9.0 rejects and leaves alone, and rejects [const] bounds, which 1.9.0 formats.

On the rust-analyzer corpus at edition 2024, the two releases give identical output on all but one of the files both accept. A reproducer for each difference, at both releases and editions 2021 and 2024, is in chloro-core/tests/conformance/rustfmt-versions/; the rustfmt versions record names each class and the rustfmt change behind it.

rustfmt 1.7.0 and earlier are refused: 1.7.0 has no 2024 Style Guide rules, and 540 of the 981 rust-analyzer files both releases accept come out differently. Nightly rustfmt is not compared.

items.title: What is not covered
items.text:
• rustfmt.toml. chloro reads no configuration file. Options come from --config or Config.
  • Unstable options. chloro always uses rustfmt's defaults for them, and setting one to another value is an error (Configuration).
  • rustfmt's command line. There are no --emit, --files-with-diff, --edition or standard input modes; --check reports a count, not a diff. Editions are set with --config edition=….
  • Out-of-line modules. rustfmt formats the files a crate's mod declarations lead to; chloro formats the files and directories you name, whatever modules they declare.
  • Syntax rust-analyzer's parser cannot represent. chloro parses with rust-analyzer's parser and rebuilds the tree for the cases where rustc's parser accepts something rust-analyzer rejects. Two such constructs remain (below).
  • Error reporting. Both tools leave a file that does not parse unchanged, but rustfmt prints the parse error and exits with status 1, while chloro reports nothing and exits with 0 (#87). Where rustfmt fails with an internal error but still writes output, chloro writes the same output and reports no error; the library has no error channel.

items.title: Known differences
items.text:
Six cases are recorded and open in the conformance ledger:

what effect 19 A doc comment before an expression in an argument list, array, let or statement position: rustc treats it as an attribute of the expression and rustfmt formats it with the expression; chloro leaves it where it is. Layout differs around the comment. No registry file is affected; rustc warns about such comments (unused_doc_comments). 20 Edition-2015 trait methods with anonymous parameters, fn f(usize);, which rust-analyzer's parser rejects. chloro returns the file unchanged; rustfmt formats it. 21 rustfmt's internal error on one file of rustyline 14.0.0. rustfmt exits with an error and writes the output chloro writes. 22 rustfmt's run time on a 47 KB generated file of pest_meta 2.9.2. rustfmt takes over nine minutes and chloro 0.2 s, for identical output. 23 Files where rustfmt's own output is not a fixed point (eight known). chloro's output matches rustfmt's at every pass. 24 Minor forms: a trailing comma in builtin # offset_of(…), which rust-analyzer rejects. chloro returns the file unchanged.

A difference not listed here is a bug: please open an issue with the input, the options, and the rustfmt version.

items.title: Reproducing the comparison
items.text:
The rustfmt on PATH is the 1.9.0 reference; rustup run 1.88.0 rustfmt is the 1.8.0 one.

cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example conform -- -i              # 1220 files against the 1.9.0 snapshots
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example conform -- -i -V 1.8.0     # the same at rustfmt_version = 1.8.0
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example config_matrix -- -n 1220   # 31 option values against live rustfmt
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example config_matrix -- --root ~/.cargo/registry/src -n 30000 default
cargo test -p chloro-core --test conformance batch                      # regenerate the snapshots

Development explains the snapshots and how they are regenerated.

items.title: Project history
items.text:
chloro keeps a development journal: dated records of what was decided, what was measured, and what was tried and did not work. This page explains how the journal is organised and where to start reading it.

The journal is the docs/journal/ directory of the repository. Entries are Markdown files named YYYY-MM-DD-title.md, written to the format in docs/JOURNAL.md: statements of what exists, with the files and figures that support them, and no recommendations.

items.text: when what happened entries November–December 2025 0.5 to 0.7: a hand-written formatter over rust-analyzer's rowan trees, matching rustfmt on 233 of 1220 conformance files the per-crate changelogs 9–11 October 2026 The rustfmt port: rustfmt 1.9.0's formatting logic ported module by module onto rust-analyzer's syntax trees, reaching 1219 of 1220. Then an investigation of where the port's time goes, and whether the proof of concept was a better foundation. It was not: most of its speed came from work it skipped. It reached 1220 of 1220, added rustfmt 1.8.0 support, and cut instructions by 66%. programme, handoff

items.title: Reading the performance programme
items.text:
The programme's records use short codes. Start with the handoff, which is written for a reader who did not follow the work: it explains every code and summarises each experiment, failure and measurement with its source.

code meaning where E1 … E31 experiments, one hypothesis each, with a written record ledger, experiments/EXP-NNN-*.md R2, R5 the conformance fixes, and the fixes for a code review's findings conformance ledger M1 … M6 the six full measurements against rustfmt on an idle machine measurements P1 … P11 the ranked list of parser-side improvements parser theory record "base", "the start" 884f9c9, release 0.8.0 "best-known-good" the latest commit whose checks were reproduced on the merged branch ledger Ir instructions executed, as counted by callgrind

Other records that are useful on their own:

  • The protocol: what counts as a result, the checks a change must pass, and how work on an approach is stopped.
  • The conformance ledger: every mismatch with rustfmt found, its root cause, and the six cases still open.
  • The rustfmt versions record: where rustfmt 1.7.0, 1.8.0 and 1.9.0 differ on real code, and why 1.7.0 is not supported.
  • The records of approaches that did not improve performance, each with the measurement that ruled it out: a faster allocator, code layout, a resident server process, scheduling, an exact width model. The handoff's sections 7 and 12 list them.

Commit hashes in the journal

The commits of the performance branch were re-recorded under the maintainer's name before the branch was merged, which gave them new hashes. The journal's references read new (was old): the commit's hash in the repository, with the hash recorded at the time beside it. Commands, file names and tool output quoted in the records keep the original hashes; 2026-10-17-commit-map.md maps every one of them.

items.title: Performance
items.text: chloro's speed and memory use measured against rustfmt, the conditions of the measurements, and what was not measured.

items.title: Summary
items.text:
Against rustfmt 1.9.0, checking already-formatted crates:

  • One core: 0.21–0.35 of rustfmt's wall time on each of nine crates, with every chloro run faster than every rustfmt run.
  • Four cores: 0.08–0.17 of rustfmt's wall time, chloro using one thread per core and rustfmt running as it does (one thread).
  • Memory: 4–10 MiB peak resident memory on one core and 5–23 MiB on four, against rustfmt's 43–86 MiB.
  • Unchanged trees: a warm --check of 1238 formatted files in 16.2 ms on four cores.

Against chloro 0.8.0, the release before the performance work, the formatter executes 66% fewer instructions on the same files and formats 2.7 times as many bytes per second on one core.

Conditions

All figures are from measurement M6 (2026-10-17), taken with benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh on an idle 4-core KVM guest (Intel Xeon, 2.80 GHz class, Linux), with rustfmt 1.9.0-stable (2d8144b788 2026-07-07) and chloro built with the workspace's release profile. Each cell is 30 timed runs with hyperfine (15 runs in each of two rounds, the command order reversed in the second), after 2 warm-up runs. Both tools check copies of the same files, formatted by rustfmt first, with --check; chloro's cache is off. One-core rows pin both tools to the same core. Ratios are of mean wall times.

Absolute times depend on this host and varied by up to 20–40% between measurement sessions, so compare the ratios, which were taken with both tools interleaved in the same session.

items.title: Instruction counts
items.text:
Wall-time measurements on a shared virtual machine are noisy, so chloro's performance work was guided by the number of instructions executed, which barely varies between runs. The counts come from callgrind (benchmarks/profile.sh) on two fixed samples of 49 files each, one from the conformance corpus and one from four crates.io crates:

sample chloro 0.8.0 now profile-guided build 49 rust-analyzer files (650 KB) 587,988,576 202,822,485 (−65.5%) 170,069,599 (−71.1%) 49 crates.io files (732 KB) 688,589,271 255,681,198 (−62.9%) 219,987,557 (−68.1%)

Of what remains, lexing and parsing are 34% of the instructions on the first sample and 42% on the second.

items.title: Profile-guided builds
items.text: benchmarks/pgo.sh builds chloro with profile-guided optimisation, training on the conformance corpus. On these measurements the profile-guided build ran in 0.18–0.33 of rustfmt's wall time on one core and 0.07–0.16 on four. The release workflow applies the same training to the targets whose runners execute them natively; see Releasing.

items.title: What was not measured
items.text:
• macOS and Windows: every figure here is from x86-64 Linux.
  • rustfmt's throughput in process: rustfmt is only timed as a process, including its start-up (loading librustc_driver costs it about 30 ms and 34 MiB).
  • Memory bandwidth, and runs on more than four cores.
  • Unformatted input. The inputs are formatted by rustfmt first, because rustfmt's --check builds a diff of every file that would change, and that would add the cost of the diff to rustfmt's time.

items.title: Optimisations
items.text: chloro makes the same formatting decisions as rustfmt, so it does the same work, with less overhead. It reads syntax from one flat array instead of pointer-linked nodes, lexes and builds the tree in one pass, memoises rewrites that deep nesting would otherwise repeat, proves from a node's tokens when a one-line layout cannot fit instead of rendering it to find out, keeps short-lived strings in a per-thread arena, formats files and large files' items on all cores, and skips files it has already seen formatted. How it works explains each of these.

items.title: Reproducing
items.text:
Needs hyperfine 2.0, taskset, jq and python3; valgrind and setarch for instruction counts; and rustfmt 1.9.0 on PATH.

cargo build --release -p chloro --features cli && cargo build --release -p chloro-core --examples
benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh -r 15 -w 2 --rounds 2 --core 3   # wall, CPU, RSS per workload; tables in report.md
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3                                 # instruction count on the 49-file sample
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- -n 5     # in-process MB/s on the corpus

Benchmarking describes the workloads and the scripts. The six measurement records, M1 to M6, and the experiments behind each change are in the project history.

items.title: Parallelism and caches
items.text: chloro can format parts of a file separately because, in rustfmt, the output of a top-level item depends only on that item, and the text between items can be filled in afterwards, in order.

items.title: Item independence
items.text:
rustfmt formats a file by walking its items in order with one visitor. Before building any parallelism, chloro tested whether each top-level item formats the same on its own as it does in its file. Splitting the rust-analyzer corpus and a crates.io corpus into units (one top-level item, or one group of use, mod x; or extern crate items that rustfmt sorts together) gave 13,650 units in the first and 965,193 in the second. Formatted on its own, every unit came out as it does in its file, except in the text before it: a comment before the item, a #[rustfmt::skip] module, a #! line. No unit differed in any other way.

So a unit's output depends only on its own text, the configuration, and the file's rustfmt::skip::macros and ::attributes names. This was an empirical test rather than a proof, so both uses below are also tested for identical output over both corpora.

items.title: Formatting items on several threads
items.text:
format_source_with_config_parallel (formatter/parallel.rs) parses the file once into one immutable tree, which the threads share: a node handle is a reference and an index, and the tree is Sync. Workers take units from a shared queue, longest first, and each formats its unit with a visitor of its own, starting from the state the sequential visitor would have at that point.

The text before each unit needs special handling. The sequential visitor writes the comments and blank lines before an item from inside the item's own code, and what it writes depends on the output so far (whether the buffer is empty, how many newlines it ends with). A worker cannot know that, so it does not write the gap: it records the call it would have made. The calling thread then walks the units in order, replays each recorded gap call on the real output buffer, and appends the unit's text.

If a unit's record cannot be placed where it belongs, the calling thread formats that part sequentially instead; a panic in a worker is re-raised with its original payload. tests/parallel_equivalence.rs checks that the two paths give identical output, and the corpus check (examples/bench --threads 4 --check) compares the parallel output of every corpus file with hashes recorded from the sequential path.

items.title: The command line's scheduler
items.text: The command line runs one worker per core and gives out files largest first from a shared queue. A file of 128 KiB or more is also split into items, on all threads; the file-level workers and the item-level threads share the cores, and the operating system schedules them. Measured with the CHLORO_TRACE timeline and rebuilt from per-thread CPU clocks, the resulting schedule is within 1–1.5% of the shortest the work allows, on every measured crate.

items.title: The fixed-point cache
items.text: The command line's cache (chloro/src/cli/cache.rs) records one fact per entry: this exact file content, formatted by this binary under this configuration, comes out unchanged. It stores no formatted text, no paths and no timestamps. The binary and the configuration select the cache file; the content digests (BLAKE3, 256 bits) are its entries. The set is read once at start-up, shared read-only by the workers, and written once at the end through a temporary file and a rename. Caching describes its behaviour and limits.

items.title: The unit cache
items.text:
format_source_with_unit_cache is the parallel function with a cache lookup before each unit is formatted. A cached unit records its output with every position relative to the unit's start, so a hit applies wherever the unit has moved in the file. Everything that depends on more than the unit is recomputed on every call: the parse, the whole-file checks, the text between units, and the final newline handling. A re-format after an edit to one item therefore costs a parse, one lookup per unit, and the edited unit.

The command line's --unit-cache stores these records in a file next to the fixed-point cache, keyed by the same binary and configuration. It was checked over both corpora, at one and four threads, to give output identical to formatting without it.

items.title: The formatting engine
items.text: chloro's formatter is a module-by-module port of rustfmt 1.9.0. An adaptation layer translates rust-analyzer's syntax tree for it, and a few additions make it faster without changing any formatting decision.

items.title: Modules ported from rustfmt
items.text:
The modules of chloro-core/src/formatter/ carry the names of the rustfmt source files they reproduce, so a decision in chloro can be compared line by line with rustfmt's:

module role formatting the entry point: parse, visit, trailing newlines, newline style visitor, missed_spans walk items and statements; copy comments and blank lines between them items, imports, reorder items, use trees, the sorting of use, mod and extern crate expr, stmt, chains, closures, matches, pairs, patterns, types expressions and their parts macros, macro_args macro calls, with their arguments re-parsed, and macro_rules! bodies overflow, lists comma-separated lists and the "overflow the last item" heuristic attr, comment attributes, doc comments, re-indenting and recovering comments skip the names listed by #[rustfmt::skip::macros(..)] and #[rustfmt::skip::attributes(..)] shape, context, utils, sort shared infrastructure, as in rustfmt

As in rustfmt, every node implements a rewrite method that takes a shape (the width available and the current indentation) and returns the node's text, or nothing if it cannot be laid out in that shape. A caller with several possible layouts tries them in rustfmt's order and keeps the first that succeeds: a call on one line, then with its last argument overflowing, then one argument per line, and so on.

Comments are handled as rustfmt handles them with its default (stable) options: re-indented and stripped of trailing whitespace, never re-wrapped.

items.title: The adaptation layer
items.text:
rustfmt is written against rustc's abstract syntax tree; chloro reads rust-analyzer's lossless tree. Three modules translate, so that the ported code can keep rustfmt's control flow:

  • span computes rustc's spans. rustfmt recovers comments, blank lines and code it gives up on by slicing the source between nodes, so spans must start and end where rustc's do. The main difference is that rust-analyzer attaches leading comments to the following item, while a rustc span starts at the first attribute.
  • nodes presents rust-analyzer's nodes in rustc's shape: doc comments as attributes, a block as a list of statements with its tail expression, rustc's classification of statements.
  • macro_args parses macro call arguments as rustc's parser would (expression, then type, pattern or item), laying each argument's tree out at its offset in the file.

items.title: Performance
items.text: rustfmt chooses a layout by rendering candidates and measuring them. Each attempt rewrites every subexpression again, so the work grows with nesting, exponentially in the worst case. chloro has to make the same choices, so it cannot skip an attempt that might succeed. It saves time by not repeating work and by skipping attempts that cannot succeed.

items.title: A memo for deep nesting
items.text: A rewrite of an expression at a given shape is stored and reused when the same expression is asked for at the same shape again. On ordinary code that rarely happens (3.2% of lookups hit), and storing every result costs about as much as the hits save, so the memo only stores rewrites nested six or more deep (MEMO_MIN_DEPTH), where most repeated attempts happen. The memo is cleared at each top-level item.

items.title: A lower bound on one-line width
items.text:
Some attempts succeed only if their result fits on one line: a closure body without braces, or if c { a } else { b } on one line. formatter/width.rs computes, from a node's tokens and without rendering anything, a width below which no one-line rendering can be: the sum of the tokens that every formatting path writes unchanged (identifiers, keywords, literals, and the punctuation each node kind always writes). When the bound already exceeds the space available, the attempt is skipped, because it would fail.

The bound is justified token class by token class in the module's documentation, and tested against every actual one-line rendering over both corpora, three option sets and synthetic worst cases (tests/width_bound.rs). Its main effect is on deeply nested closures: a 2,000-byte file of closures nested 16 deep went from 105.4 million instructions to 5.7 million.

One case is also decided by structure alone: a closure body that renders a match with an arm is never one line. The argument for this comes from rustfmt's rewrite_match, and debug builds check it on every rewrite.

items.title: Fewer, cheaper allocations
items.text:
• Lists are written into the caller's buffer instead of being assembled and copied.
  • Intermediate values that never leave one module (a call's list items, a chain's entries, a path's segments) live in a per-thread bumpalo arena, reset at each top-level item (formatter/scratch.rs), instead of being separate heap allocations. The arena uses no unsafe code.
  • Dozens of local fast paths in the comment scanner, the list formatter and string building avoid re-scanning text, each tested against the computation it replaces. One of them is chloro-core's only unsafe block: a 16-byte SSE2 load in the comment scanner, used only where the target supports it, with a randomised test against the scalar search.

None of these changes affects what a rewrite returns. Each was checked by formatting both corpora and comparing every file's output with the output recorded before the change.

items.title: Modules not from rustfmt
items.text:
• width and scratch, above.
  • parallel and unit_cache: formatting top-level items on several threads, and reusing formatted items. See Parallelism and caches.
  • rustc_compat and rustc_syntax: the boundary between what rustc's parser and rust-analyzer's accept. See Parsing.
  • printer: a public Printer trait from chloro's pre-port formatter. Nothing in the formatter calls it; it is kept for API compatibility.

items.title: How it works
items.text: chloro is rustfmt's formatting code ported onto a parser that is available as an ordinary library, then optimised. This page gives an overview of how a file goes from source text to formatted output.

items.title: Background
items.text:
rustfmt is built on the Rust compiler: it parses a file with rustc's parser into rustc's abstract syntax tree, then rewrites each node, trying candidate layouts in a fixed order and keeping the first that fits the width. Its output is the product of a few hundred interacting width heuristics and fallbacks. chloro's first versions tried to reproduce that output rule by rule from observation, and matched rustfmt on 233 of the 1220 conformance files. Reproducing a few hundred interacting heuristics one rule at a time from their output did not come close to rustfmt.

So chloro ports rustfmt instead. The formatter in chloro-core follows rustfmt 1.9.0's source module by module, keeping its control flow, names and comments, so that every formatting decision can be checked against the rustfmt code it reproduces. The difference is the parser: the syntax comes from rust-analyzer's parser (ra_ap_parser), which is published as a library, rather than from rustc, which is not. A thin adaptation layer presents rust-analyzer's syntax in the shape rustfmt's code expects.

The port matched rustfmt on 1219 of the 1220 files, and later on all 1220. The performance work that followed left every output byte unchanged and made the formatter 2.7 times as fast.

items.title: The pipeline
items.text:
The formatting pipeline Source text is normalised, lexed, parsed by rust-analyzer's parser into a flat syntax tree, checked and repaired against what rustc's parser accepts, then walked by the visitor, whose ported rustfmt rewrites produce the output, which gets rustfmt's trailing newline and line endings. Source text drop BOM, CRLF → LF normalize_src Lexer rustc_lexer, one pass cst::lex Parser rust-analyzer's grammar ra_ap_parser Flat syntax tree one array, Copy handles cst::Tree rustc's view repair or reject rustc_syntax rustc_compat Visitor items and gaps, in order visitor missed_spans Rewrites rustfmt's modules, ported expr, items, chains, lists, overflow, … Output newlines, line endings apply_newline_style

From source text to formatted text. Each box names the module that does the step.

  1. Normalise. A leading byte order mark is dropped and \r\n reads as \n, as rustc's source map does.
  2. Lex and parse. chloro's own lexer front end turns the text into rust-analyzer's tokens in one pass over rustc_lexer, and rust-analyzer's parser turns them into a stream of events. A text with a lexer error goes through rust-analyzer's own lexer instead, so errors are reported the same way.
  3. Build the tree. The parser's events become one flat array of nodes and tokens over the source text, with comments and whitespace attached where rust-analyzer attaches them. Parsing and the syntax tree describes the tree.
  4. Match rustc's parser. rustfmt formats exactly the files rustc's parser accepts, and the two parsers do not accept exactly the same syntax. Where rust-analyzer rejects syntax rustc accepts, the tree is rebuilt with the node rustc would build (rustc_syntax); where rust-analyzer accepts syntax rustc rejects, the file is returned unchanged (rustc_compat). A file that neither parser accepts is returned unchanged, as rustfmt returns it.
  5. Visit and rewrite. The visitor walks items and statements in source order, copying the comments and blank lines between them from the source, and the ported rewrite modules format each node. The formatting engine describes this part.
  6. Finish. Trailing newlines are trimmed to one and line endings set by newline_style, as rustfmt's format_lines and apply_newline_style do.

For a file of 128 KiB or more, step 5 runs on several threads at once, one top-level item per task, while the text between items is written in order on one thread. Parallelism and caches covers that, and the caches that let chloro skip work it has done before.

items.title: Where the time goes
items.text:
On the 49-file instruction-count sample, after the performance work:

part share of instructions lexing and parsing, including building the tree 34% (42% on a crates.io sample) the visitor and rewrites most of the rest memory allocation about 12%, spread across both

The parser is rust-analyzer's, used as published. Its remaining cost could be cut further only with a fork of ra_ap_parser (sizing its buffers up front and writing chloro's tree directly from its events), which would save at most about 6–7% of the total; chloro does not maintain a fork.

items.title: The crates
items.text:
crate what is in it chloro-core the lexer front end and flat tree (cst), the formatter (formatter), and the public entry points chloro the command line (src/cli/: argument parsing, file discovery, the worker pool, the caches) and a library facade over chloro-core

chloro-core's runtime dependency tree is 18 crates as cargo tree counts them (itself included), rust-analyzer's parser and its lexer among them; syn is not one of them. rowan and ra_ap_syntax, the tree types rust-analyzer itself uses, are only development dependencies: the tests use them to check that chloro builds the same tree as rust-analyzer.

items.title: Parsing and the syntax tree
items.text: chloro parses with rust-analyzer's parser and stores the result as one flat array, so that reading a node of the tree is an array lookup that allocates nothing.

items.title: Why rust-analyzer's parser
items.text:
rustfmt parses with rustc's parser, which is only available inside the compiler. Of the parsers available as ordinary crates, rust-analyzer's (ra_ap_parser) is the one written to the same grammar and kept current with it, and it is lossless: every byte of the source, comments and whitespace included, belongs to a token in the tree. rustfmt depends on that information, because it recovers comments and blank lines by slicing the source between nodes.

The parser is used as published, pinned to one version (0.0.307 today) in chloro-core/Cargo.toml. It produces a stream of events (start node, token, finish node, error); chloro does everything after that, from building the tree to formatting.

items.title: The lexer front end
items.text:
rust-analyzer's own lexing step (LexedStr) restarts rustc_lexer at every token, converts each token kind, collects error messages, and then walks the tokens a second time to build the parser's input. chloro's cst::lex does both in one loop, into buffers sized from the text, and recognises the most common tokens (whitespace, ASCII identifiers, one-character punctuation, line comments) with a byte scan, handing the rest to rustc_lexer's cursor.

It must produce exactly the tokens LexedStr produces, and two checks ensure that it does:

  • Any text with a lexer error, a shebang or front matter goes to LexedStr as before, so error handling is rust-analyzer's own.
  • examples/lex_equality.rs compares every token, every parser input call and the parser's output with LexedStr's, over both corpora in two editions, 10,000 random texts and 10,000 mutated corpus files; and debug builds compare the two on every text they lex.

With this lexer, formatting the crates.io sample takes 15% fewer instructions.

items.title: The flat tree
items.text:
cst::Tree is the whole file as one Vec of 16-byte elements in preorder: each element is a node or a token, with its kind, its byte range in the source, and the index just past its subtree. Children are found by skipping subtrees; a token's text is a slice of the source, so no text is copied.

     source: fn main() {}

index  kind              range   end
0      SOURCE_FILE       0..12   14
1        FN              0..12   14
2          FN_KW         0..2    3
3          WHITESPACE    2..3    4
4          NAME          3..7    6
5            IDENT       3..7    6
6          PARAM_LIST    7..9    9
7            L_PAREN     7..8    8
8            R_PAREN     8..9    9
9          WHITESPACE    9..10   10
10         BLOCK_EXPR    10..12  14
11           STMT_LIST   10..12  14
12             L_CURLY   10..11  13
13             R_CURLY   11..12  14

The tree of fn main() {}, as cst::Tree::parse builds it. end is the index after the element's subtree, so the next sibling of NAME (index 4) is at index 6.

A handle to a node or token (Node, Token) is a reference to the tree and an index. It is Copy, and making one allocates nothing. In rowan, the tree library rust-analyzer itself uses, reading a node creates a reference-counted "red" node on the heap. Replacing rowan's trees with this array cut the formatter's instructions by a quarter and its heap allocations by 43%.

On top of the array, a typed layer (cst::ast) has the same names as rust-analyzer's ra_ap_syntax::ast: ast::Fn, expr.lhs(), item.name(), block.stmt_list(). Its 501 accessors are generated from rust-analyzer's grammar file (cst/rust.ungram) by cst/gen_ast.py, and a test checks that the generated file is up to date.

The tree is built in one pass from the parser's events, attaching comments and whitespace to nodes by the rules rust-analyzer uses. Tests compare the result element by element with the tree rust-analyzer's own code builds through rowan, on every corpus file; debug builds make the same comparison on every tree they build.

items.title: Macro arguments
items.text: rust-analyzer keeps the body of a macro call as an opaque token tree. rustfmt formats a call like foo!(a + b, Vec<u8>) by parsing each comma-separated argument as an expression, a type, a pattern or an item, in that order. chloro does the same with rust-analyzer's parser, and lays each argument's tree out at its original offset in the file, so spans, comments and source slices work inside macro arguments exactly as elsewhere. These fragment trees live in an arena that lasts for one formatting run.

items.title: Where the two parsers disagree
items.text:
rustfmt formats only what rustc's parser accepts, and leaves everything else alone. The two parsers accept almost the same syntax, with differences in both directions:

  • rust-analyzer accepts, rustc rejects. rust-analyzer is deliberately permissive (it parses broken code in an editor) and accepts some removed or experimental syntax. formatter/rustc_compat.rs lists the rustc parse errors that matter, such as <- as an operator, a..= without an end, or misplaced doc comments, and returns such a file unchanged, as rustfmt would. Some of these rules depend on the rustfmt release being reproduced, because rustc 1.88's parser and rustc 1.97's differ.
  • rustc accepts, rust-analyzer rejects. For a few constructs, such as a parenthesised first bound in a trait object (Box<(Copy) + Send>), a float literal used as a field name, or a const block as an item, formatter/rustc_syntax.rs rebuilds the tree with the node rustc would build, so the file is formatted as rustfmt formats it.

Two constructs remain where rust-analyzer's parser has no node to build; they are listed as known differences.

items.title: Installation
items.text: chloro is published as two crates: chloro, which holds the command-line tool and a small library facade, and chloro-core, the formatter itself.

items.title: The command-line tool
items.text:
BinarySourceCheckout 
cargo binstall chloro

cargo-binstall downloads the binary attached to the GitHub release for your platform. The 0.8.0 release has binaries for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc and aarch64-pc-windows-msvc; on any other platform cargo binstall falls back to building from source.

cargo install chloro --features cli

The binary is behind the cli feature, so that a library dependency on chloro does not pull in the command line's dependencies. Building needs Rust 1.88 or later (the workspace's rust-version).

git clone https://github.com/lmmx/chloro
cd chloro
cargo install --path chloro --features cli

Check that it runs:

chloro --help

The release profile builds with fat link-time optimisation and one codegen unit, which makes a from-source build slower than a default release build. Release binaries for the targets that GitHub's runners execute natively can also be built with profile-guided optimisation; see Releasing.

items.title: The library
items.text:
Add chloro to your Cargo.toml for the formatting functions and Config:

[dependencies]
chloro = "0.8"

chloro re-exports format_source, format_source_with_config and Config from chloro-core. The parallel and cached entry points, and the syntax tree, are only in chloro-core:

[dependencies]
chloro-core = "0.8"

Both crates have no default features. The Library guide shows what each entry point does, and the Rust API reference lists them with links to docs.rs.

Versions

The performance work and the rustfmt 1.8.0 support described on this site are on the main branch and not yet in a published release; 0.8.0 is the latest release. The Changelog says which version each change is in.

items.title: Run-time requirements
items.text: chloro has no run-time dependencies. It does not call rustfmt, rustc or cargo, and it reads no configuration file: options come from --config on the command line or from Config in the library. Apart from the files it formats, the only file it writes is its cache, which lives in the user cache directory by default.

items.title: Quickstart
items.text: How to check and format a crate with chloro, and how to run the check in CI. Each command gives the same result as rustfmt at edition 2024 with default options.

items.title: Check
items.text:
From the root of a crate:

$ chloro --check src/ tests/ examples/

Error: 3 file(s) need formatting

--check formats every .rs file under the paths you name, writes nothing, and exits with status 1 if any file's formatted text differs from what is on disk. Every path must exist: a missing one is an error before anything is formatted. Add --verbose to see each file as it is processed and a summary at the end.

Name your source directories

chloro walks every directory under the paths it is given, hidden directories and target/ included, and does not read .gitignore. With no path at all it starts at the current directory. In a Cargo project, pass src/ and your other source directories rather than ., or target/ will be formatted too (#90).

items.title: Format
items.text:
chloro --write src/ tests/ examples/

--write rewrites each file whose formatted text differs, and leaves the others untouched. Without --check or --write, chloro prints each formatted file to standard output, which is useful for a single file:

chloro src/lib.rs | diff src/lib.rs -

items.title: Choose options
items.text:
chloro takes rustfmt's stable options by rustfmt's names, as comma-separated key=value pairs:

chloro --config max_width=80,tab_spaces=2 --write src/
chloro --config edition=2021 --check src/
chloro --config rustfmt_version=1.8.0 --check src/

An unknown option, a malformed value or an unstable rustfmt option set away from its default stops the run before any file is read:

$ chloro --config wrap_comments=true src/
Error: invalid --config: `wrap_comments` is an unstable rustfmt option; only its default `false` is supported

chloro does not read rustfmt.toml. If your project has one, translate its stable options into --config; Configuration lists every option chloro accepts.

items.title: Use it in CI
items.text:
A GitHub Actions job that fails when a file is not formatted:

jobs:
  format:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@v2
        with:
          tool: cargo-binstall
      - run: cargo binstall --no-confirm chloro
      - run: chloro --check --no-cache src/ tests/

--no-cache is optional. A CI runner starts with an empty cache, so the cache has nothing to answer from; in the measurements a cold cache cost 364 ms against 356 ms without one on a 1238-file tree (see Caching).

items.title: Call it from Rust
items.text:
let mut config = chloro::Config::default();
config.set("max_width", "80").unwrap();
let formatted = chloro::format_source_with_config("fn main(){let x=1;}", &config);
assert_eq!(formatted, "fn main() {\n    let x = 1;\n}\n");

The Library guide covers the rest of the API, including formatting one large file on several threads.

items.title: Caching
items.text: Most formatter runs, from a pre-commit hook or an editor on save, are over files that are already formatted. chloro records which file contents it has seen come out unchanged and skips them on later runs.

items.title: The fixed-point cache
items.text:
When chloro finds a file already formatted, it records the file's BLAKE3 digest. On a later run, a file whose digest is recorded is reported as formatted without being parsed. The digest is recorded only for content observed to be a fixed point: a file left unchanged by the run, or a file just written whose formatted text formats to itself.

The cache is on by default for --check, --write and printing. It never changes what chloro does: the output and the exit status of a run are the same with and without it.

On the 1238 already-formatted files of the conformance corpus, on four cores:

run wall time --check, warm cache 16.2 ms --check, cache directory removed before the run 364 ms --check --no-cache 356 ms --check with chloro 0.8.0, which has no cache 1014 ms

These figures are from measurement M6; the Performance page describes the conditions.

items.title: What the key covers
items.text:
Each cache file holds the digests for one chloro binary and one configuration:

  • The binary. The BLAKE3 digest of the running executable, with the crate version, the cache format version and the target. Rebuilding or upgrading chloro starts a new cache file, so a digest recorded by one build is never trusted by another.
  • The configuration. Every field of the Config built from --config, serialised field by field. Changing an option starts a new cache file.
  • The content. The digest of the file's exact bytes. Paths and timestamps of source files are not recorded, so renaming or touching a file does not invalidate it.

Hashing the 2 MB executable on every run would cost more than the rest of a small run, so its digest is recorded under the executable's identity (path, size and modification time, and on Unix also device, inode and status-change time) and read back while that identity is unchanged.

Limitation

An executable rewritten in place with every one of those identity fields unchanged would be taken for the binary recorded earlier. On Unix that requires a write within the file system's timestamp granularity of the previous change, a clock set back, or a write that bypasses the file system; on Windows, where the identity is path, size and modification time, a same-size rewrite with the modification time restored. Use --no-cache, or remove the cache directory, if you replace chloro's binary by such means.

items.title: Where the cache lives
items.text:
chloro uses the first of these that is set:

  1. --cache-dir DIR
  2. $CHLORO_CACHE_DIR
  3. $XDG_CACHE_HOME/chloro
  4. %LOCALAPPDATA%\chloro\cache on Windows
  5. ~/Library/Caches/chloro on macOS
  6. ~/.cache/chloro

If none can be resolved, the run proceeds without a cache. --verbose prints the cache file in use and how many entries it holds.

The directory holds *.chloro-cache files (one per binary and configuration), *.chloro-exe records of executable digests and, with --unit-cache, *.chloro-units files. A cache file keeps at most 131,072 digests, dropping the least recently seen; files not written for 30 days are removed by later runs. Writes go to a temporary file that is renamed into place, so concurrent runs do not corrupt a cache; deleting the directory at any time is safe.

items.title: Turning it off
items.text:
chloro --no-cache --check src/

--no-cache neither reads nor writes any cache, the unit cache included.

items.title: The unit cache
items.text:
--unit-cache adds a second, opt-in cache, for files that did change. It keeps the formatted text of each top-level item (or each group of use, mod and extern crate items that rustfmt sorts together), keyed by the item's text, the whole configuration and the file's rustfmt::skip names. When a file changes, only the items not seen before are formatted; the rest of the file (the parse, the checks that apply to the whole file, the text between items) is recomputed every time, so the result is exactly what formatting the whole file gives. This was verified over the conformance corpus and a registry corpus of 25,077 files, at one and four threads.

chloro --unit-cache --write src/

It is off by default because it costs more than it saves when it starts empty: a cold --check of the conformance corpus took 10–15% longer with it, and its file grew to 8.6 MB for that corpus. It helps when the same large files are reformatted after small edits. In process, reformatting a large file after a one-item edit took 0.26–0.47 of the time of formatting it from scratch; at the command line, process start-up and reading the cache take back part of that saving. The records are capped at 64 MiB per cache file.

The library exposes the same mechanism, with a store you provide; see the library guide.

items.title: Command line
items.text:
chloro formats the .rs files under the paths you give it. Depending on the flags, it prints the formatted files, checks them against what is on disk, or writes them back.

chloro [OPTIONS] [SOURCES]...

items.title: Sources
items.text:
Each source is a file or a directory. A directory is walked recursively for files ending in .rs; a file named directly is formatted whatever its extension. With no source, chloro starts at the current directory.

  • Every directory under a source is walked, including hidden ones and target/. chloro has no ignore rules and does not read .gitignore, so in a Cargo project name src/, tests/, examples/ and benches/ rather than . (#90).
  • A file reachable twice (named twice, reached through a symlink, or both named and found in a directory) is formatted once.
  • A symlinked directory that points back into a directory being walked is not followed again.
  • A source path that does not exist is an error, reported before any file is formatted.

items.title: Modes
items.text:
--check Format every file and compare. Nothing is written. Exits with status 1 and Error: N file(s) need formatting when at least one file would change. --write Write each file whose formatted text differs from its contents. Files that are already formatted are not touched. (neither) Print every formatted file to standard output, one after another. With more than one thread, files are printed in the order they finish, which can vary from run to run; use --threads 1 for a stable order, or name one file.

With both --check and --write, files are written and the exit status reports whether any needed formatting.

items.title: Exit status
items.text:
status when 0 every file was processed; with --check, none needs formatting 1 --check found files that need formatting; or a file could not be read or written; or a source path does not exist; or --config was invalid; or the arguments could not be parsed

A file that does not parse, or that contains syntax rustc's parser rejects, is left unchanged, as rustfmt leaves it. Unlike rustfmt, which prints the parse error and exits with status 1, chloro does not report such a file, even with --verbose, and counts it as formatted; that is a known issue (#87). A file with an inner #![rustfmt::skip] attribute is also left unchanged.

items.title: Options
items.text:
The flags are summarised here; the CLI reference has the full help text.

option what it does guide -c, --check exit 1 if any file would change; write nothing above -w, --write write formatted files in place above -v, --verbose report each file, the cache in use, the thread count and a summary, on standard error --config OPTS rustfmt options as key=value,key=value Configuration --threads N worker threads (default: one per core) Parallelism --no-cache neither read nor write the caches Caching --unit-cache also cache each formatted top-level item Caching --cache-dir DIR where the caches live Caching -V, --version print the version, marked -dev unless built from the release Reference -h, --help print the help text

The default source in --help

The help text describes the default source as 'src'; the default is in fact the current directory (.), as described above (#91).

items.title: Environment variables
items.text: variable effect CHLORO_CACHE_DIR the cache directory when --cache-dir is not given XDG_CACHE_HOME when set, the default cache directory is $XDG_CACHE_HOME/chloro (on every platform) CHLORO_TRACE=FILE write a per-file, per-worker timeline of the run to FILE (a diagnostic for scheduling)

items.title: Byte order marks and line endings
items.text:
chloro handles both as rustfmt does:

  • A byte order mark at the start of a file is dropped.
  • Line endings follow the newline_style option. The default, Auto, uses the style of the file's first line ending (\r\n or \n), or the platform's for a file without one, as rustfmt does; Unix and Windows force one and Native uses the platform's.

A few things rustfmt does that chloro does not (reading rustfmt.toml, --emit, formatting standard input) are listed under rustfmt compatibility.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
chloro accepts rustfmt's stable options, with the same names, value spellings and defaults. It adds one option, rustfmt_version, which selects the rustfmt release to reproduce.

With no options, chloro formats as rustfmt --edition 2024 does with no rustfmt.toml.

items.title: Setting options
The options

option default values max_width 100 unsigned integer hard_tabs false true, false tab_spaces 4 unsigned integer newline_style Auto Auto, Native, Unix, Windows use_small_heuristics Default Default, Max, Off fn_call_width from use_small_heuristics (60) unsigned integer attr_fn_like_width from use_small_heuristics (70) unsigned integer struct_lit_width from use_small_heuristics (18) unsigned integer struct_variant_width from use_small_heuristics (35) unsigned integer array_width from use_small_heuristics (60) unsigned integer chain_width from use_small_heuristics (60) unsigned integer single_line_if_else_max_width from use_small_heuristics (50) unsigned integer; 0 always breaks single_line_let_else_max_width from use_small_heuristics (50) unsigned integer; 0 always breaks reorder_imports true true, false reorder_modules true true, false remove_nested_parens true true, false short_array_element_width_threshold 10 unsigned integer match_arm_leading_pipes Never Always, Never, Preserve fn_params_layout (or fn_args_layout) Tall Compressed, Tall, Vertical match_block_trailing_comma false true, false edition 2024 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024 style_edition follows edition 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024 merge_derives true true, false use_try_shorthand false true, false use_field_init_shorthand false true, false force_explicit_abi true true, false disable_all_formatting false true, false rustfmt_version 1.9.0 1.8.0, 1.9.0 (chloro only)

Each option means what it means in rustfmt; the rustfmt configuration reference describes them. rustfmt compatibility lists the option values on which chloro's output has been compared with rustfmt's.

items.title: Width heuristics
items.text:
The eight width options, fn_call_width to single_line_let_else_max_width, are derived from max_width unless set, as in rustfmt:

  • use_small_heuristics = Default uses the values in brackets above at max_width = 100, scaled by max_width / 100 (rounded to the nearest tenth) when max_width is larger.
  • Max sets each to max_width.
  • Off sets each to 0.

An explicitly set width wins over the heuristic and is capped at max_width.

items.title: Editions
items.text: edition is the Rust edition the source is parsed as: it decides what is a keyword and what syntax is accepted. style_edition is the edition of the Rust Style Guide the output follows. As in rustfmt, an unset style_edition follows edition, so edition=2021 alone formats with the 2021 style. Style editions 2015, 2018 and 2021 are the same style; 2024 differs from them.

items.title: rustfmt_version
items.text:
This option is specific to chloro. It selects the rustfmt release whose output is reproduced:

  • 1.9.0, the default: rustfmt 1.9.0-stable (2d8144b788 2026-07-07), the release chloro is ported from.
  • 1.8.0: rustfmt 1.8.0-stable (6b00bc3880 2025-06-23), as shipped with Rust 1.88.0.

The two releases differ in a handful of formatting decisions and in which syntax their parsers accept; rustfmt compatibility lists the differences. 1.7.0 and earlier are rejected with an explanation: rustfmt 1.7.0 has no 2024 Style Guide rules, and its output differs from 1.9.0's too widely to reproduce with a few version checks in the formatter.

items.title: Unstable rustfmt options
items.text:
rustfmt's unstable options (those that need nightly rustfmt) are not configurable. chloro always behaves as rustfmt does with each at its default. Naming one with its default value is accepted, so a configuration written for stable rustfmt still works; any other value is an error:

$ chloro --config wrap_comments=true src/
Error: invalid --config: `wrap_comments` is an unstable rustfmt option; only its default `false` is supported
The unstable options and the defaults chloro applies
