items.title: Attributes in the source
items.text:
chloro honours rustfmt's attributes:

  • #![rustfmt::skip] as an inner attribute of a file leaves the file as written.
  • #[rustfmt::skip] on an item, statement or expression leaves that node as written.
  • #[rustfmt::skip::macros(name, …)] and #[rustfmt::skip::attributes(name, …)] leave calls of those macros, or those attributes, as written inside the item they are on; as inner attributes (#![…]) they apply to the whole file or module.

items.title: Library
items.text: Each of chloro's library functions takes source text and returns formatted text. None of them reads or writes files, and none starts a thread unless you ask for threads.

items.title: Which crate
items.text:
crate what it gives you chloro format_source, format_source_with_config, Config; and the command line behind the cli feature chloro-core all of the above, plus the parallel and cached entry points, parse_only, and the syntax tree

chloro re-exports these items from chloro-core, so both crates use the same Config type. The examples on this page that use only format_source* and Config work with either.

items.title: Format a string
items.text:
let formatted = chloro::format_source("fn main(){let x=1;}");
assert_eq!(formatted, "fn main() {\n    let x = 1;\n}\n");

format_source formats with rustfmt's defaults at edition 2024, the same as format_source_with_config(source, &Config::default()).

The formatting functions do not return errors. Source that does not parse, or that rustc's parser would reject, comes back unchanged, as rustfmt leaves such a file alone; so does a file with an inner #![rustfmt::skip] attribute, or any file when disable_all_formatting is set. To find out whether anything changed, compare the output with the input:

let source = "fn main() {\n    let x = 1;\n}\n";
let needs_formatting = chloro::format_source(source) != source;
assert!(!needs_formatting);

// Not valid Rust: returned as written.
let broken = "fn main( {";
assert_eq!(chloro::format_source(broken), broken);

As in rustfmt, a byte order mark is dropped and \r\n in the input reads as \n; the output's line endings are set by newline_style (by default, those of the input's first line).

items.title: Options
items.text:
let mut config = chloro::Config::default();
config.set("max_width", "80").unwrap();
config.set("edition", "2021").unwrap();
config.set("rustfmt_version", "1.8.0").unwrap();

let formatted = chloro::format_source_with_config("fn main(){}", &config);
assert_eq!(formatted, "fn main() {}\n");

// Unknown and unstable options are errors, with a message to show the user.
assert!(config.set("max_widht", "80").is_err());
assert!(config.set("wrap_comments", "true").is_err());

Config::set takes rustfmt's option names and value spellings; the fields of Config can also be set directly. Configuration lists every option.

items.title: One large file on several threads
items.text:
use chloro_core::{Config, format_source_with_config, format_source_with_config_parallel};

let source = "use std::fmt;\nfn a(){}\nfn b(){}\nstruct S{x:u8}\n";
let config = Config::default();

let parallel = format_source_with_config_parallel(source, &config, 4);
assert_eq!(parallel, format_source_with_config(source, &config));

format_source_with_config_parallel formats the file's top-level items on up to threads scoped threads, started for the call and joined before it returns. The output is identical to format_source_with_config's. With threads <= 1, or a file with fewer than two top-level items, no thread is started.

Starting threads costs more than it saves on a small file, and a program formatting many files usually does better to format several files at once with the sequential function. The command line splits only files of 128 KiB and more; see Parallelism.

items.title: A cache of formatted items
items.text:
format_source_with_unit_cache is the parallel function with a cache of formatted top-level units, which you provide by implementing UnitCache. Each unit the cache does not hold is formatted and offered to insert; each one it does hold is reused. The output is identical to format_source_with_config's.

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::collections::HashMap;

use chloro_core::{CachedUnit, Config, UnitCache, UnitKey, format_source_with_unit_cache};

/// Units in memory, keyed by everything a unit's output depends on.
#[derive(Default)]
struct MemoryUnits(RefCell<HashMap<(Vec<u8>, String), CachedUnit>>);

impl UnitCache for MemoryUnits {
    fn get(&self, key: &UnitKey<'_>) -> Option<CachedUnit> {
        let key = (key.context().to_vec(), key.text().to_owned());
        self.0.borrow().get(&key).cloned()
    }

    fn insert(&self, key: &UnitKey<'_>, unit: CachedUnit) {
        let key = (key.context().to_vec(), key.text().to_owned());
        self.0.borrow_mut().insert(key, unit);
    }
}

let units = MemoryUnits::default();
let config = Config::default();

let before = "fn a(){}\nfn b(){}\n";
let after = "fn a(){}\nfn b(){1}\n"; // only `b` changed

assert_eq!(format_source_with_unit_cache(before, &config, 1, &units), "fn a() {}\nfn b() {}\n");
// The second call formats `b` and reuses `a`.
assert_eq!(format_source_with_unit_cache(after, &config, 1, &units), "fn a() {}\nfn b() {\n    1\n}\n");

The rules for an implementation:

  • get may return a unit only if insert was given it for a key with equal context() and text(). Keying by both, or by a collision-resistant hash of both, satisfies this.
  • The key does not identify the build of chloro-core. A cache kept across processes must also be keyed by the build (the command line names its cache file by the digest of its executable). CachedUnit::to_bytes and CachedUnit::from_bytes serialise a unit for such a store.
  • The formatter calls the cache from the calling thread only, so the implementation needs no synchronisation of its own.

items.title: Parse without formatting
items.text:
use chloro_core::{Config, parse_only};

let elements = parse_only("fn main() {}", &Config::default());
assert!(elements.is_some());
assert_eq!(parse_only("fn main( {", &Config::default()), None);

parse_only runs the steps formatting starts with (normalisation, lexing, parsing, building the syntax tree, and the checks for syntax rustc's parser handles differently) and returns the number of nodes and tokens in the file's tree, or None where formatting would return the source unchanged without formatting it. It exists to measure the parser's share of the formatter's cost, and to check quickly whether chloro would format a file at all.

items.title: Debug output
items.text: chloro_core::chloro_debug! prints to standard error when debug output is enabled, either with the CHLORO_DEBUG environment variable at start-up or with chloro_core::debug::set_debug(true). It is for developing chloro itself.

items.title: The syntax tree
items.text: chloro_core::cst is the flat syntax tree the formatter reads, with a typed layer that keeps rust-analyzer's ast names. It is public so that the tools in chloro-core/examples can use it, and is not re-exported by chloro. Parsing and the syntax tree describes it.

items.title: Parallelism
items.text: By default chloro uses every core. Files are spread across worker threads, and a large file has its top-level items formatted on several threads at once. The output is identical whatever the number of threads.

items.title: Files in parallel
items.text:
The command line starts one worker per core (std::thread::available_parallelism), or --threads N workers. The files are sorted by size, largest first, and handed out from a shared queue: each worker takes the next file as soon as it finishes one. Starting with the large files keeps one late, large file from leaving the other cores idle at the end of a run.

chloro --check src/                 # one worker per core
chloro --threads 2 --check src/     # two workers
chloro --threads 1 --check src/     # sequential

rustfmt formats the files of a crate on one thread. On the nine crates of the performance measurements, chloro on four cores took 0.08–0.17 of rustfmt's wall time, against 0.21–0.35 on one core.

items.title: Large files
items.text:
A file of 128 KiB or more is also split: its top-level items are formatted on up to --threads threads, while the text between the items (comments, blank lines, items left as written) is written in order on one thread and the formatted items are put back between it. The threshold is a constant of the command line (PARALLEL_ITEMS_MIN_BYTES); below it, starting threads for one file costs more than it saves when the other cores are already busy with other files.

On the five largest files of the conformance corpus, formatting each file alone with four threads was 1.1–1.7 times as fast as with one, for 1.09–1.32 times the CPU time.

Splitting a file does not change its output, because in rustfmt the output of a top-level item depends only on the item's own text and the configuration. The exceptions are the text between items, and groups of use, mod and extern crate items, which rustfmt sorts together. chloro keeps both on the calling thread and treats a sortable group as a single unit. Parallelism and caches explains how the pieces are put back together and how that is tested.

The library exposes the same split as format_source_with_config_parallel; the library never starts threads unless asked.

items.title: Output order
items.text: With --check or --write the order in which files finish does not matter. When printing to standard output, each file is written as soon as it is formatted, so with several threads the order of the files can vary between runs (the bytes of each file do not). Use --threads 1 when the order matters.

items.title: Seeing the schedule
items.text: CHLORO_TRACE=FILE makes the command line write a timeline of the run: when each worker took each file, and when it read, hashed and formatted it. The scripts under benchmarks/schedule/ turn a trace into per-worker idle time and the length of the run's tail. On the measured crates the schedule came within 1–1.5% of the shortest possible for the work, so there is little to gain from changing it.

items.title: Benchmarking
items.text:
chloro's performance work uses two kinds of measurement: instruction counts, which are repeatable on any machine, and wall-time comparisons with rustfmt, which need an idle machine and are compared only as ratios.

The scripts are in benchmarks/; benchmarks/README.md documents every option. They need a release build of both crates first:

cargo build --release -p chloro --features cli
cargo build --release -p chloro-core --examples

items.title: Instruction counts: profile.sh
items.text:
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3 --sample-list benchmarks/samples/registry49.txt
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3 --runs 3 --per-file
benchmarks/profile.sh --core 3 --runs 3 --per-file --phase parse

profile.sh runs the CLI under valgrind's callgrind and reports the instructions executed (Ir). Two samples of 49 files are used, and a change is judged on both:

  • the fixture sample, every 25th file of the conformance corpus (650 KB);
  • the registry sample, 49 files from tokio, regex-syntax, clap_builder and winnow (benchmarks/samples/registry49.txt, 732 KB), so that a change tuned on one sample is checked on code it was not tuned on.

Counts repeat to within about 2,000 instructions from run to run, so changes far below timing noise are visible. The script does two things to keep the counts stable:

  • The script stages the binary and the sample under fixed-length paths and runs with address randomisation off (setarch -R) and an empty environment, because path lengths shift the heap's layout and with it the count.
  • --per-file formats each file in its own process and sums the counts, which removes the effect one file's allocations have on the next file's. A change of less than about 2 million instructions is judged on the per-file figure.

--phase parse counts only the parse (chloro_core::parse_only), to see the parser's share. --sim adds callgrind's cache and branch simulation; --shuffle N repeats the count with randomised code layouts, to tell a real change from an effect of code layout.

Needs valgrind and setarch.

items.title: Against rustfmt: compare_rustfmt.sh
items.text:
benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh --list                              # the workloads
benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh -r 15 -w 2 --rounds 2 --core 3      # the full comparison
benchmarks/compare_rustfmt.sh -r 5 --rounds 2 fx-hir fx-hir-ty    # some workloads
python3 benchmarks/report.py benchmarks/results/<stamp>           # tables from a run

The script times rustfmt and chloro with hyperfine on the same files: nine crates (five from rust-analyzer, four from crates.io), 287 small files, a 13-byte file for start-up, single large files through standard input, and in-process runs. For each workload it holds equal:

  • the bytes: both tools read copies of the same files, by default formatted by rustfmt first, because rustfmt's --check builds a diff of every file that would change;
  • the file set: taken from rustfmt's own list of the files it formats, then verified;
  • the configuration: defaults for both, with an empty config file for rustfmt;
  • the order: the command order is reversed in alternate rounds;
  • the output: before timing, each command runs once and must succeed; whether the two outputs agree is recorded per workload.

It records wall time, CPU time and peak memory for each run under benchmarks/results/<UTC stamp>/, and report.py turns that into tables. Pinned rows (--core) put both tools on one core; unpinned rows let chloro use every core.

Needs hyperfine 2.0, taskset, jq, python3, and rustfmt 1.9.0 (the script resolves the real binary behind rustup's proxy).

Wall time on a shared machine

Timings of the same binary on the same files varied by 20–40% between measurement sessions on the virtual machine chloro was measured on. Compare tools within one run, never across runs, and treat a wall-time change smaller than the run-to-run spread as no change.

items.title: On any Cargo project: just vs-rustfmt
items.text:
just vs-rustfmt path/to/project      # chloro, chloro --threads 1 and cargo fmt
just vs-ruff                         # the same on ruff, in ~/tmp/ruff (cloned if missing)
just vs-ruff ~/src/ruff 10           # another checkout, 10 runs

These recipes (.just/bench.just) give both tools the same files: the list cargo fmt --all formats, so each file is formatted once. A plain rustfmt over every .rs file of a project formats each module file several times, because rustfmt also formats the modules a file declares; on ruff that is 3.6 passes per file. Both tools run in check mode, so use an already-formatted tree. They need hyperfine.

They time the chloro on your PATH, first making sure it was built from this checkout. just reinstall installs the CLI with a build ID baked in, which chloro --version prints (chloro 0.8.0-dev (2f9b060, build <id>)); just build-id computes the ID of the checkout as it is on disk, from the content of every file that goes into the binary (committed or not), Cargo.lock, the toolchain and the install command. When the two match, the benchmark starts at once without running Cargo; when they differ, or the installed chloro has no build ID, the recipe runs just reinstall first, outside the timed runs.

items.title: In process: bench
items.text:
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- -n 5                # MB/s on the corpus
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --root ~/.cargo/registry/src
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --phase parse       # the parse alone

bench times format_source over every file, excluding I/O and process start-up, and reports the best of -n rounds. It also records and checks output hashes (Development).

items.title: Other tools
items.text: tool what it is for benchmarks/cliffs/ synthetic inputs of 20 shapes at growing sizes, fitted for how instruction counts scale, to find inputs where the work grows faster than the input benchmarks/schedule/ turning a CHLORO_TRACE timeline into per-worker idle time, and rebuilding the schedule from CPU clocks examples/alloc_count.rs counting allocations alloc-timing, alloc-mimalloc, alloc-jemalloc, alloc-snmalloc features instrumenting or replacing the global allocator in measurement builds; all off by default

items.title: Measurement records
items.text: Six full measurements against rustfmt (M1 to M6) and the experiments behind each change are in the journal; the project history explains how to find them. The Performance page summarises the latest.

items.title: Development
items.text: How the repository is laid out, how to build and test it, and the checks a change must pass. A change that alters any formatted output is a conformance change and must say so; any other change must leave every output byte unchanged.

items.title: Layout
items.text: path what is there chloro-core/src/cst/ the lexer front end (lex.rs), the flat syntax tree (mod.rs), and the typed layer (ast.rs, generated.rs from gen_ast.py and rust.ungram) chloro-core/src/formatter/ the ported rustfmt modules, the adaptation layer, parallel.rs, unit_cache.rs, width.rs chloro-core/tests/ unit and integration tests, and the conformance suite under tests/conformance/ chloro-core/examples/ the measurement and comparison tools (conform, config_matrix, bench, lex_equality, unit_cache, …) chloro/src/cli/ the command line: arguments, file discovery, the worker pool, the caches, the trace benchmarks/ the benchmark harness against rustfmt, the instruction-count profiler, the PGO build script docs/site/ this website's sources; zensical.toml at the root configures it docs/journal/ the development journal: design records, experiments and measurements, in the format of docs/JOURNAL.md

items.title: Building and testing
items.text:
cargo build --workspace --all-features
cargo test --workspace --all-features

The Justfile wraps the usual commands: just test (with cargo nextest), just clippy (-D warnings, all targets and features), just check, just docs (rustdoc). Formatting and lint hooks run through prek or pre-commit: just install-hooks, then just precommit. Commit messages follow Conventional Commits, enforced by a commit-msg hook, because the release tooling builds the changelog from them.

README.md and chloro/README.md are kept identical (just docs-match checks; just docs-mirror copies the newer over the older): the second is the README crates.io shows for chloro.

items.title: Conformance
items.text:
The conformance suite lives in chloro-core/tests/conformance/:

  • fixtures/rust-analyzer/ holds 1238 .rs files from rust-analyzer, the corpus.
  • snapshots/ra/<crate>/<case>.rustfmt.rs holds rustfmt 1.9.0's output for each, or the input itself where rustfmt rejects the file. snapshots/ra-1.8.0/ holds rustfmt 1.8.0's output where it differs from 1.9.0's.
  • rustfmt-versions/ holds a reproducer for each class of difference between rustfmt 1.8.0 and 1.9.0.

conform compares chloro with the stored snapshots, without running rustfmt:

cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example conform -- -i            # 1.9.0
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example conform -- -i -V 1.8.0   # 1.8.0

It reports the number of identical files, diff totals, files that are not idempotent (-i), and throughput. The batch test regenerates the snapshots with the rustfmt on PATH, and writes chloro's output and a diff beside each:

cargo test -p chloro-core --test conformance batch

For the parser and syntax crates (581 small cases) only the .rustfmt.rs files are tracked; the outputs and diffs are written locally and ignored by git. just conf summarises the current diffs, and just conf-plain prints the summary without colour.

config_matrix compares option values and other corpora against a live rustfmt:

cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example config_matrix -- -n 1220
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example config_matrix -- --root ~/.cargo/registry/src -n 30000 default

The registry corpus is the 577 crates named in docs/journal/2026-10-14-autoresearch/corpus/registry-manifest.toml, fetched into the cargo registry.

items.title: Checks for a change
items.text:
A change that is meant to leave the output alone (a performance change, a refactor) must show that it does. In order, cheapest first:

  1. cargo fmt --check, just clippy, cargo test --workspace --all-features.

  2. Output hashes. Record the hash of every corpus file's output before the change, and check them after:

    cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --record before.tsv   # on the base
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --check before.tsv    # on the change
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example bench -- --threads 4 --check before.tsv

    Zero files may change, sequentially or with four threads. Add --root ~/.cargo/registry/src to do the same over the registry corpus.

  3. conform -i at both rustfmt releases: no fewer identical files, none non-idempotent.

  4. config_matrix -n 1220: no option value loses a file.
  5. For a performance claim, the instruction count on both samples (Benchmarking).

A conformance fix changes outputs on purpose: the files it changes should be exactly the ones it targets, checked file by file, and the case recorded in the conformance ledger.

items.title: Code conventions
items.text:
• rustfmt's structure. Formatter modules keep rustfmt's module, function and variable names and its control flow, so that a difference can be traced to the rustfmt code it reproduces. Optimisations are written so that this correspondence stays readable.
  • Public API. Changes are additive: format_source and format_source_with_config keep their signatures, and new capabilities are new functions.
  • unsafe code. chloro forbids it. chloro-core has one unsafe block, with a written safety argument and a randomised test. Any new one needs the same, and a safe alternative measured first.
  • Dependencies. A new dependency needs a measured reason. chloro-core has 18 crates in its runtime tree.

items.title: The journal
items.text: docs/journal/ records design decisions, experiments and measurements as dated entries, in the format docs/JOURNAL.md describes. The journal records why things are the way they are; this website describes how chloro works now. The project history is a guide to the journal.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: Where chloro's documentation lives, and how this website is built, checked and published to GitHub Pages.

items.title: Where documentation lives
items.text:
where for source this website, https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/ using and maintaining chloro: guides, compatibility, performance, architecture docs/site/, zensical.toml docs.rs/chloro, docs.rs/chloro-core the Rust API, item by item doc comments in the code README.md a first look on GitHub and crates.io, with links here README.md, mirrored to chloro/README.md CHANGELOG.md what changed in each release, for users; shown on the Changelog page CHANGELOG.md docs/journal/ the record of decisions, experiments and measurements dated Markdown entries, see the project history

Each fact should be documented in one place. The website describes what chloro does and links to the journal for the evidence, rather than copying experiment records.

items.title: Building the site
items.text:
The site is built with Zensical, as the documentation of nave is. It needs only uv:

just site-serve        # live preview at http://localhost:8000/chloro/
just site-build        # build into site/ (ignored by git)

The recipes pin Zensical's version (ZENSICAL in .just/site.just), and the deployment workflow pins the same one. To upgrade, change both and check the site.

items.title: Checks
items.text:
just site-check        # nav, links and the CLI help snippet
just site-examples     # compile and run every Rust example
  • site-check builds the site, then runs docs/scripts/check_site.py: every page is in the nav and every nav entry exists; every internal link, image and stylesheet of the built site resolves, anchors included, under the /chloro/ base path the site is served from; and docs/site/_snippets/cli/help.txt matches the current chloro --help. Zensical's own build also reports links to missing pages and anchors.
  • site-examples runs docs/scripts/check_examples.py, which turns every fenced rust block under docs/site/ into a test of a scratch crate (in target/docs-examples/) that depends on the workspace's crates, and runs them. A block is the body of a test function, as in a doctest, so it can declare items and assert! its results.

When the CLI's help text changes, just site-snippets regenerates the snippet that the CLI reference includes.

items.title: Writing pages
items.text:
• Pages are Markdown with the extensions configured in zensical.toml: admonitions (!!! note), tabs (=== "Title"), collapsible blocks (??? info), definition lists, footnotes, and keys (++"--check"++ renders a flag as a key cap). --8<-- "path" includes a file, relative to the repository root.
  • Add a new page to the nav in zensical.toml; site-check fails on a page that is not in it.
  • Link between pages with relative paths to the .md files. Link to the journal, the source and anything else in the repository with absolute GitHub URLs on master, since those files are not part of the site.
  • State measured figures with their conditions, and link to the record they come from.

items.title: Design
items.text: The site follows the design of nave's documentation: Zensical's modern theme, Instrument Serif for page titles, Encode Sans Condensed for headings, Work Sans for text, commands set as key caps. chloro's own colours are chlorophyll greens, defined as CSS variables for the light and dark schemes in docs/site/assets/stylesheets/extra.css, with a toggle in the header. The mark in docs/site/assets/images/chloro.svg is a leaf whose veins branch like a syntax tree. Charts and diagrams are inline SVG drawn with the page's colour variables, so they follow the scheme, and each chart has its data in a table beside it.

items.title: Deployment
items.text:
GitHub Pages serves the site from the gh-pages branch (Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source: Deploy from a branch, gh-pages, / (root)). .github/workflows/site.yml writes to that branch:

  • Production. Every push to master builds the site and deploys it to the root of gh-pages, which is served at https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/. The deploy replaces everything at the root except the pr-preview/ directory.
  • Pull request previews. A pull request that changes the site (docs/site/, zensical.toml, CHANGELOG.md, docs/scripts/ or the workflow) is built with its site_url set to its preview path and deployed to gh-pages/pr-preview/pr-<number>/, served at https://lmmx.github.io/chloro/pr-preview/pr-<number>/. The workflow posts the link as a comment on the pull request once GitHub Pages has published it, edits that same comment on later pushes, and deletes the preview when the pull request is closed or merged.

Every pull request also runs the build and docs/scripts/check_site.py, whether or not it gets a preview. Pull requests from forks get the checks but no preview: their workflows have a read-only token and cannot push to gh-pages. The job that deploys a preview checks out the default branch, not the pull request, and publishes only the files the build job produced.

The production and preview deploys write to separate paths of the branch, and each rebases and retries if the branch moved while it ran, so they can run at the same time. The gh-pages branch keeps every deploy as a commit.

The workflow reads the Pages source at the start of each run. While the source is still GitHub Actions, it also publishes master with actions/deploy-pages and does not deploy previews; once the source is the gh-pages branch, that job is skipped. The workflow can also be run by hand from the Actions tab.

items.title: Upgrading the parser
items.text: chloro reimplements two pieces of rust-analyzer's parser crate for speed: its lexing step and its tree building. Both are pinned to the behaviour of one ra_ap_parser release, so after a version bump they must be checked against the new release.

items.title: What is pinned
items.text:
dependency version why chloro depends on its exact behaviour ra_ap_parser 0.0.307 the grammar; cst::lex reproduces its LexedStr::new and to_input, and TreeBuilder::steps_fused reproduces its intersperse_trivia ra-ap-rustc_lexer 0.137.0 the tokeniser cst::lex drives directly, the same version ra_ap_parser uses rustc-literal-escaper 0.0.4 literal validation, as in LexedStr ra_ap_syntax, rowan (dev) 0.0.307, 0.15.15 the reference the equality tests compare chloro's tree with cst/rust.ungram copied from the ra_ap_syntax 0.0.307 crate the grammar the typed layer is generated from

The three runtime crates are upgraded together: ra-ap-rustc_lexer and rustc-literal-escaper are the versions ra_ap_parser itself depends on.

items.title: The equality harnesses
items.text:
Each reimplementation has a harness that compares it with the code it replaces. Release builds do not run these comparisons; debug builds also run them inline, on every input.

what harness what it compares the lexer front end (cst/lex.rs) examples/lex_equality.rs every token's kind and offset, every call that builds the parser's input, and the parser's output, against LexedStr and to_input; over the corpus in editions 2021 and 2024, 10,000 random texts and 10,000 mutated corpus files in all four editions the lexer front end, inline debug builds of cst::lex the same comparison on every text a debug build lexes the fused tree build (TreeBuilder::steps_fused) cst tests fused_build_equals_the_interspersed_build* the fused build against the build through rust-analyzer's intersperse_trivia, on sample sources and every corpus file the flat tree as a whole cst tests flat_tree_equals_the_rowan_tree* chloro's tree against the rowan tree ra_ap_syntax builds, node by node the fused build, inline debug builds of TreeBuilder::steps the fused build against intersperse_trivia on every tree a debug build makes the typed layer cst::ast test generated_layer_is_up_to_date the checked-in generated.rs against gen_ast.py's output

items.title: Bumping ra_ap_parser
items.text:
1. Bump the versions together. In chloro-core/Cargo.toml, set ra_ap_parser and the development dependencies ra_ap_syntax and rowan to the new release's versions, and ra-ap-rustc_lexer and rustc-literal-escaper to the versions the new ra_ap_parser depends on (cargo tree -p ra_ap_parser).

  2. Regenerate the typed layer. Copy rust.ungram from the root of the new ra_ap_syntax crate (in the cargo registry once the dependency is fetched) over chloro-core/src/cst/rust.ungram, and run the generator, passing ra_ap_syntax's own generated nodes so the script checks that the accessor set matches:

    python3 chloro-core/src/cst/gen_ast.py chloro-core/src/cst/rust.ungram \
    chloro-core/src/cst/generated.rs \
    ~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-*/ra_ap_syntax-<version>/src/ast/generated/nodes.rs

    It prints any difference and exits with 1 if there is one.

  3. Read the diffs of the reimplemented code. In the new ra_ap_parser, compare lexed_str.rs (LexedStr::new), shortcuts.rs (to_input, intersperse_trivia) and the trivia attachment rules with the previous release. A change there needs the same change in cst/lex.rs or cst/mod.rs; the module documentation of each names the source it follows.

  4. Run the harnesses.

    cargo test -p chloro-core --lib cst                         # tree equality, generated layer
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example lex_equality   # 0 mismatches required
cargo run --release -p chloro-core --example lex_equality -- --root ~/.cargo/registry/src
cargo run -p chloro-core --example bench -- -n 1            # debug build: every inline check, on the corpus

    Each prints its mismatches and exits with 1 if there is any. The debug bench run is slow; it is the one that exercises the inline checks on every file.

  5. Run the conformance checks. A parser change can change what parses. Record output hashes on the old version, then compare on the new one, and rerun conform and config_matrix as in Development. Any output that changes needs to be explained by a change in rust-analyzer's grammar, and compared with rustfmt.

  6. Check the rustc boundary. formatter/rustc_compat.rs and formatter/rustc_syntax.rs encode where rust-analyzer's parser and rustc's disagree. A new release may close a gap (a rustc_syntax rebuild is no longer needed) or open one; the conformance ledger lists the cases each rule covers.

Release builds do not check

The inline comparisons run only in debug builds. A release build on a new parser version that skipped step 4 would silently produce whatever the stale reimplementation produces.

items.title: Releasing
items.text: chloro is released with release-plz from the master branch. Both crates are released together at the same version, each gets a tag and a GitHub release, and publishing the chloro release builds the binaries.

items.title: Release process
items.text:
just ship            # release-plz picks the version from the commits
just ship 0.9.0      # or set it

just ship refuses to run unless master is checked out and up to date with origin/master. It then:

  1. dry-runs the publish (release-plz release --dry-run);
  2. bumps the versions of chloro and chloro-core and updates each crate's CHANGELOG.md from the Conventional Commit messages (release-plz update, grouped by release-plz.toml);
  3. runs just prepush (check, clippy, rustdoc) and commits the bump;
  4. pushes, and runs release-plz release, which publishes both crates to crates.io and creates the tags (chloro-v<version>, chloro-core-v<version>) and GitHub releases.

just ship-manual is a fallback for when release-plz is not working.

items.title: Before a release
items.text:
The repository has no CI workflow that runs the tests on pull requests, so the release commit must be checked by hand:

  • [ ] cargo test --workspace --all-features and just clippy pass.
  • [ ] The conformance checks pass: conform -i at 1.9.0 and 1.8.0 (1220 of 1220, none non-idempotent) and config_matrix -n 1220 (Development).
  • [ ] If ra_ap_parser changed since the last release, the parser harnesses were run.
  • [ ] The root CHANGELOG.md: move the Unreleased entries under the new version and date. The per-crate changelogs are written by release-plz; the root one is written by hand for users.
  • [ ] The README badges (dependency count, binary size) are current: just emblazon.
  • [ ] README.md and chloro/README.md are identical (just docs-match); the second is what crates.io shows.
  • [ ] The website's Installation note about unreleased features, and the release named there, are updated.

items.title: Binaries
items.text:
Publishing the GitHub release for a chloro-v* tag runs .github/workflows/binaries.yml, which builds the CLI for each target and attaches the archives to the release. Their names match the [package.metadata.binstall] section of chloro/Cargo.toml, which is how cargo binstall chloro finds them.

target runner build x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu ubuntu-22.04 profile-guided x86_64-apple-darwin macos-13 profile-guided aarch64-apple-darwin macos-13 plain (cross-compiled) x86_64-pc-windows-msvc windows-2022 profile-guided, static CRT aarch64-pc-windows-msvc windows-2022 plain (cross-compiled), static CRT

Each target's job may fail without failing the others. The 0.8.0 release has archives only for the Linux and Windows targets; check whether the macos-13 runner is still available before relying on macOS binaries.

items.title: Profile-guided builds
items.text:
benchmarks/pgo.sh builds chloro with profile-guided optimisation: it compiles an instrumented binary (-Cprofile-generate), runs it over the conformance corpus with --check and through bench, merges the profile with llvm-profdata (from the llvm-tools-preview component), and builds again with -Cprofile-use.

benchmarks/pgo.sh                                  # local profile-guided build
benchmarks/pgo.sh --phase train --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
benchmarks/pgo.sh --phase use --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

The release workflow runs the training phase on each target whose runner executes it natively and sets RUSTFLAGS so the upload step's build uses the profile. A cross-compiled target, or one whose training fails, gets the plain build with a warning in the log. On the measurements, the profile-guided build executed 16% fewer instructions than the plain one and ran in 0.80–0.95 of its wall time, with identical output.

Not yet exercised by a release

The profile-guided step was added after 0.8.0 and has been validated by running its commands locally on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, not by a release run. On the first release that uses it, read each target's log for PGO skipped, PGO training failed, and no profile data available warnings from the compiler.

items.title: Versions
items.text: Both crates share a version (0.8.0 at the latest release). chloro depends on chloro-core at the same version through the workspace's [workspace.dependencies]. The minimum supported Rust version is the workspace's rust-version, 1.88.

items.title: Rust API
items.text:
The Rust API is documented on docs.rs. This page lists the public entry points and where each is explained on this site.

docs.rs/chloroThe library facade and the command-line crate. docs.rs/chloro-coreThe formatter, its entry points, the configuration and the syntax tree.

items.title: Formatting
items.text:
item in chloro in chloro-core format_source(source: &str) -> String yes yes rustfmt's defaults, edition 2024 format_source_with_config(source: &str, config: &Config) -> String yes yes any options format_source_with_config_parallel(source, config, threads) -> String yes top-level items on up to threads threads; guide format_source_with_unit_cache(source, config, threads, cache: &dyn UnitCache) -> String yes reuses formatted items; guide parse_only(source, config) -> Option<usize> yes the parse alone; guide

Every formatting function returns the source unchanged when it does not parse, when rustc's parser would reject it, when it has an inner #![rustfmt::skip], or when disable_all_formatting is set. All of them return the same text for the same source and configuration.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
item Config one public field per stable rustfmt option, plus rustfmt_version; Default is rustfmt's defaults Config::set(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) -> Result<(), String> set an option by rustfmt's name and spelling chloro_core::formatter::config::{NewlineStyle, Heuristics, Edition, StyleEdition, MatchArmLeadingPipe, Density, RustfmtVersion} the enum-valued options

Configuration lists every option and its default.

items.text: item trait UnitCache { fn get(&self, key: &UnitKey<'_>) -> Option<CachedUnit>; fn insert(&self, key: &UnitKey<'_>, unit: CachedUnit); } the store format_source_with_unit_cache reads and fills UnitKey what a unit's output depends on: context() (configuration, skip names, crate version) and text() CachedUnit one formatted unit; to_bytes and from_bytes serialise it

items.title: chloro
items.text: Reference for the chloro command. The Command line guide explains how the options work together.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
Usage: chloro [OPTIONS] [SOURCES]...

A Rust code formatter reproducing `rustfmt --edition 2024`.

Arguments:
  [SOURCES]...       Path(s) to file(s) or directory to format (default: 'src')

Options:
  -c, --check        Check if files need formatting (exit 1 if so)
  -w, --write        Write formatted output back to files
  -v, --verbose      Show verbose output
      --config OPTS  rustfmt options as comma-separated key=value pairs
      --no-cache     Format every file; do not read or write the caches
      --unit-cache   Also cache each formatted top-level item, so that a changed
                     file formats only the items not seen before (off by default)
      --cache-dir D  Cache directory (default: $CHLORO_CACHE_DIR, else the
                     user cache directory, e.g. ~/.cache/chloro)
      --threads N    Threads to use (default: one per core)
  -V, --version      Print the version and exit
  -h, --help         Show this help message

Examples:
  # Format a single file and print to stdout
  chloro src/lib.rs

  # Format multiple files
  chloro src/*.rs

  # Check if files need formatting
  chloro --check src/

  # Format files in-place
  chloro --write src/

  # Format with rustfmt options
  chloro --config max_width=80,tab_spaces=2 src/lib.rs

Cache:
  chloro records the content hash of every file it finds already formatted,
  keyed by the chloro binary and the --config options, and skips formatting
  files whose content it has seen formatted before. The output and exit code
  are the same with and without the cache.

  With --unit-cache, chloro also keeps the formatted output of each top-level
  item (or group of `use`/`mod`/`extern crate` items) under the same key and
  the item's text, and formats only the items of a changed file it has not
  seen. The output and exit code are the same. It is off by default: a run that
  finds nothing in it (a cold CI run) costs 10-15% more with it on.

Note

[SOURCES] defaults to the current directory (.), not 'src' as the help text says (#91).

items.title: --check / -c
items.text: Format every file without writing anything. Exit with status 1, and print Error: N file(s) need formatting, if any file's formatted text differs from its contents.

items.title: --write / -w
items.text: Write each file whose formatted text differs from its contents. Without --check or --write, every formatted file is printed to standard output.

items.title: --config OPTS
items.text: rustfmt options as comma-separated key=value pairs, with rustfmt's names and value spellings, plus rustfmt_version. An invalid option is an error before any file is read. Configuration lists them.

items.title: --threads N
items.text: The number of worker threads. The default, or 0, is one per core. Files of 128 KiB and more also have their top-level items formatted on this many threads. Parallelism.

items.title: --no-cache
items.text: Neither read nor write the fixed-point cache or the unit cache. Caching.

items.title: --unit-cache
items.text: Also cache the formatted text of each top-level item, so that a changed file formats only the items not seen before. Off by default; overridden by --no-cache. Caching.

items.title: --cache-dir DIR
items.text: The directory of the caches. Default: $CHLORO_CACHE_DIR, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/chloro, else the platform's user cache directory (~/.cache/chloro, ~/Library/Caches/chloro, %LOCALAPPDATA%\chloro\cache).

items.title: --verbose / -v
items.text: Report, on standard error, the sources and mode, the cache file and its size, the number of files and threads, each file as it is processed, and a summary at the end.

items.title: --version / -V
items.text:
Print the version and exit. The plain version, chloro 0.8.0, is printed only by a build of the release itself; any other build is marked as a development build, with what is known of its source:

output built from chloro 0.8.0 the release: the commit tagged chloro-v0.8.0 with no uncommitted changes, or the crate published to crates.io chloro 0.8.0-dev (2f9b060) another commit (2f9b060) of a git checkout chloro 0.8.0-dev (2f9b060, dirty) a checkout with uncommitted changes to the files that go into the binary chloro 0.8.0-dev (unknown source) a copy of the source with no git repository or packaging record, which cannot be checked

The version is the crate's version; -dev is added only to this output. The check is made when chloro is compiled (chloro/build.rs), from the local repository: the build reruns when HEAD moves, a tag changes, or a source file changes, and --version reads nothing at run time.

A binary installed with just reinstall also prints its build ID, a hash of the source it was built from, as in chloro 0.8.0-dev (2f9b060, dirty, build <id>) (Benchmarking).

items.title: --help / -h
items.text: Print the help text and exit.

items.title: Exit status
items.text: status meaning 0 success; with --check, nothing needs formatting 1 --check found files to format, or a file could not be read or written, or a source does not exist, or --config or the arguments were invalid

items.title: Environment
items.text: variable effect CHLORO_CACHE_DIR the cache directory, when --cache-dir is not given XDG_CACHE_HOME the parent of the default cache directory, when set CHLORO_TRACE a file to write a per-worker timeline of the run to
